issues.legal_issue: Property remaining in an executrix’s administration does not become a legatee’s property merely because the executrix deposits it with court officials under court orders, and it cannot be attached as the legatee’s property.
material_facts: The executrix held assets that remained part of the unadministered estate.
Under court orders, she delivered the assets to court officials, who were not acting on behalf of the legatee.
The State admitted that the delivered assets were unadministered assets in the executrix’s hands.
issues.conclusion: The assets remained part of the unadministered estate and could not lawfully be attached as the alleged contemner’s property.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 87 and 88 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, property may be attached as the property of the person whose appearance is sought. Property held by an executrix becomes vested in a legatee only when delivered to that legatee or to someone acting on the legatee’s behalf; delivery to court officials acting against the legatee’s interests does not effect that transfer.

rule.if: contempt_proceeding and executrix_administered_estate_assets and court_ordered_delivery_to_officials and not delivery_to_beneficiary

predicates.contempt_proceeding: The court was dealing with a proceeding alleging contempt and seeking the alleged contemner’s appearance.
predicates.executrix_administered_estate_assets: An executrix held assets that remained under administration as part of an estate.
predicates.court_ordered_delivery_to_officials: The executrix delivered the assets to court officials in obedience to the court’s order.
predicates.delivery_to_beneficiary: The assets were delivered to the beneficiary or to someone acting on the beneficiary’s behalf.

issues.definition: When an executrix’s estate assets are delivered to court officials rather than to the beneficiary, those assets are not attachable as the alleged contemner’s property in a contempt proceeding.

issues.legal_issue: The statutory proclamation and attachment procedure for securing a person’s appearance is unavailable in contempt proceedings.
material_facts: A person alleged to have committed contempt did not appear despite notices requiring him to attend court.
The court used a proclamation and property attachment procedure under the criminal procedure code to seek his appearance.
issues.conclusion: Sections 87 and 88 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, could not be used to secure the appearance of a person alleged to have committed contempt.
issues.legal_principle: The Code of Criminal Procedure does not apply to contempt proceedings, and sections 87 and 88 are therefore unavailable to secure an alleged contemner’s presence. The Court followed Sukhdev Singh Sodhi v. The Chief Justice and Judges of the Pepsu High Court, [1954] S.C.R. 454. Although a court of record has powers necessary and incidental to its contempt jurisdiction, the Court did not decide whether those powers include attachment of an alleged contemner’s property.

predicates.contempt_proceeding: The proceeding concerned an allegation of contempt of court.
predicates.alleged_contemner_failed_to_appear: The person alleged to have committed contempt did not attend court when required to do so.
predicates.court_used_criminal_procedure_to_secure_: The court invoked a criminal procedure for compelling the alleged contemner’s attendance.

issues.definition: When a person alleged to have committed contempt fails to appear, the criminal procedure for compelling attendance cannot be used in the contempt proceeding.

issues.legal_issue: An order treating property attached in a contempt proceeding as being at the government’s disposal does not give the government lawful possession or control of that property.
material_facts: Property was attached in a proceeding seeking the appearance of a person alleged to have committed contempt.
The court later directed that the attached property be made over to the government under the criminal procedure code.
The government received and retained the property, although it had no independent claim to it.
issues.conclusion: The government had no authority under section 88(7) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, to take or retain the property, and the court could not make the property over to it.
issues.legal_principle: Section 88(7) provides for government disposal of property attached under section 88 when the proclaimed person does not appear. Because sections 87 and 88 are unavailable in contempt proceedings, section 88(7) cannot authorize government possession in such a proceeding. Even if a court of record has an inherent power to attach property to secure an alleged contemner’s appearance, that power does not include a right to make the property over to the government.

predicates.contempt_proceeding: The property was dealt with in a proceeding alleging contempt of court.
predicates.property_attached_to_secure_appearance: The court attached property for the purpose of securing the alleged contemner’s appearance.
predicates.government_received_attached_property: The government took possession of property that had been attached by the court.

issues.definition: When the government receives property attached to secure an alleged contemner’s appearance in a contempt proceeding, the attachment does not give the government lawful control of it.

issues.legal_issue: An attachment made to secure an alleged contemner’s appearance cannot continue after the alleged contemner dies, and the rightful owner is then entitled to restoration.
material_facts: The court attached property for the purpose of securing the alleged contemner’s appearance.
The alleged contemner died while the property remained attached and in government possession.
The claimant sought restoration of property to which the claimant had a rightful claim.
issues.conclusion: Even assuming the attachment had been valid, it could not continue after the alleged contemner’s death, and the rightful owner was entitled to restoration of the property.
issues.legal_principle: An attachment made to secure a person’s appearance serves no purpose once that person has died. Even if the attachment was valid, it can subsist only while the alleged contemner is alive; on the contemner’s death, the rightful owner is entitled to restoration.

rule.if: contempt_proceeding and attachment_to_secure_appearance and alleged_contemner_died and claimant_has_rightful_claim

predicates.contempt_proceeding: The attachment arose in a proceeding alleging contempt of court.
predicates.attachment_to_secure_appearance: The property was attached to secure the alleged contemner’s appearance.
predicates.alleged_contemner_died: The person whose appearance the attachment was intended to secure died while the property remained attached.
predicates.claimant_has_rightful_claim: The claimant had a rightful claim to the property held under the attachment.

issues.definition: When an alleged contemner dies, an attachment made to secure that person’s appearance ends, and a claimant with a rightful claim to the property is entitled to its restoration.

issues.legal_issue: A court may and should correct its own erroneous order that placed property belonging to a rightful claimant in the government’s possession, rather than require the claimant to rely solely on a civil suit.
material_facts: The court’s orders led to property being transferred to the government, which had no independent claim to it.
The court later found that the property had been wrongly attached and transferred.
The rightful claimant applied to the court for restoration of the property.
issues.conclusion: The court had to correct its mistake and order the property restored to the rightful claimant; a civil suit was not the only remedy in these circumstances.
issues.legal_principle: A court’s duty is to ensure that its acts do no injury to suitors. The inherent jurisdiction to correct an error is not generally available merely because a court has wrongly decided a matter within its jurisdiction, but that limitation does not apply where the court’s erroneous act placed property in the possession of a government that was not a claimant to it. The Court relied on Rodger v. Comptoir d’Escompte de Paris, [1871] L.R. 3 P.C. 465, 475.

rule.if: application_to_correct_court_caused_property_transfer and court_discovered_its_error and government_is_not_a_claimant and claimant_has_rightful_claim

predicates.application_to_correct_court_caused_prop: A claimant applied to the court to restore property transferred to the government as a result of the court’s own orders.
predicates.court_discovered_its_error: The court found that its orders had wrongly caused the property to be attached or transferred.
predicates.government_is_not_a_claimant: The government held the property but had no independent claim to it.
predicates.claimant_has_rightful_claim: The person seeking restoration had a rightful claim to the property.

issues.definition: When a rightful claimant asks a court to correct its own error that placed property with a government that has no claim to it, the court must correct the error and order restoration.
